To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interactions between carbon and nitrogen availability regulate soil trace gas fluxes, including CO2 (carbon dioxide) and N2O (nitrous oxide).
carbon and nitrogen (C and N) availability interact to influence greenhouse gas (GHg) emissions.

1) the response of CO 2 emissions to N addition was highly sensitive to the level of available C, 2) the response of N 2 O emissions to N addition depended strongly on C availability, and 3) the interaction of C and N availability caused ~60 and 5 times the total CO 2 and CO 2 plus N 2 O emission, respectively, compared to either C or N addition alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of stoichiometric gradients of carbon (C) and/or nitrogen (N) availability on the emission of CO2 and/or N2O.
the effects of stoichiometry of C and N availability on CO2 and N20 fluxes.
the effects of stoichiometry on greenhouse gas emissions and biogenic carbon and nitrogen cycles in soils.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the response of soil trace gas fluxes to C and N availability is highly variable and depends upon the level of C and N availability.
the interactions of C and N availability regulate CO2 and N fluxes, but the direction and intensity of the regulation depends on the relative availability of the two elements.
the interaction between C and N availability can have significant impact on soil GHG emission.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
C or N addition alone may be a useful strategy to mitigate CO2 and N 0 emissions, but the combined application of C and N may result in higher emissions.

C and N availability interact in a complex and nonlinear manner that can be explained by changes in the use efficiency of C and N, and this interaction is important for understanding and modeling GHG fluxes from soil.
the stoichiometric ratio between C and N availability can significantly affect CO2 and N ₂ O fluxes, which is important to understand the biogeochemical cycles of C, N and GHG emissions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C and N interactions can have large impacts on GHG emissions from soils, and that these interactions should be accounted for in models and in field experiments.
the response of trace gas fluxes along stoichometric gradients in C or N availability should be considered when modeling GHG emissions.
N and C availability interact in a non-linear fashion to affect GHG emissions, and the stoichiometry of C and N should be considered in future biogeochemical modeling efforts.
